items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The energy transferred when a gas changes volume, W = pΔV at constant pressure and in general the area under the p–V curve"?
items.answer: work done by a gas
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of work done by a gas.

items.stem: Explain, using the first law, why a gas cools when it expands rapidly.
items.answer: In a rapid expansion there is little time for thermal energy transfer (Q ≈ 0); the gas does work on the surroundings, so ΔU = −W is negative and its temperature falls.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In a rapid expansion there is little time for thermal energy transfer (Q ≈ 0); the gas does work on the surroundings, so ΔU = −W is negative and its temperature falls. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Supplying heat to a gas always increases its temperature." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: If the gas does at least as much work as the heat supplied (e.g. isothermal expansion), its internal energy and temperature need not rise.
items.markingKey: If the gas does at least as much work as the heat supplied (e.g. isothermal expansion), its internal energy and temperature need not rise. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the work done by the gas.
0.5 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 40 K. Calculate the thermal energy supplied.
items.markingKey: ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, W = pΔV = nRΔT (M1); Q = (5/2)nRΔT = 416 J (A1).

items.stem: 0.50 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is heated at a constant pressure of 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa from 300 K to 450 K. (a) Calculate the increase in internal energy. (b) Calculate the change in volume and the work done by the gas. (c) Calculate the thermal energy supplied. (d) Explain why more heat is needed than for the same temperature rise at constant volume.
items.answer: (a) ΔU = 1.5 × 0.50 × 8.31 × 150 = 935 J; (b) ΔV = nRΔT/p = 5.19 × 10⁻³ m³, W = 623 J; (c) Q = 1560 J; (d) at constant pressure the gas also does work expanding, so extra energy must be supplied.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔU = 1.5 × 0.50 × 8.31 × 150 = 935 J; (b) ΔV = nRΔT/p = 5.19 × 10⁻³ m³, W = 623 J; (c) Q = 1560 J; (d) at constant pressure the gas also does work expanding, so extra energy must be supplied.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas"?
options: A graph of pressure against volume on which a process is shown as a curve and the work done is the area under it
The total random kinetic energy of its atoms, U = (3/2)nRT = (3/2)Nk_BT
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases; equivalently, thermal energy cannot spontaneously flow from a colder to a hotter body
A process at constant temperature, for which ΔU = 0 and Q = W; pV = constant for an ideal gas
items.answer: The total random kinetic energy of its atoms, U = (3/2)nRT = (3/2)Nk_BT
items.markingKey: B. "internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas" is the total random kinetic energy of its atoms, U = (3/2)nRT = (3/2)Nk_BT.

items.stem: Chloé writes four statements while revising first law of thermodynamics, work done by a gas and internal energy. Which one is a misconception?
options: Entropy (J K⁻¹) measures the number of microscopic arrangements available, i.e. how dispersed energy is; it is not an amount of energy.
Temperatures must be in kelvin; using °C gives wrong (even negative) efficiencies.
In the first law Q = ΔU + W, W is the work done on the gas.
If the gas does at least as much work as the heat supplied (e.g. isothermal expansion), its internal energy and temperature need not rise.
items.answer: In the first law Q = ΔU + W, W is the work done on the gas.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: In the IB convention, W is the work done by the gas; work done on the gas is −W.

items.stem: An ideal gas is taken through a complete cycle back to its initial state. Over the cycle, ΔU is
items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: B. U is a state function.

items.stem: Distinguish between work (W) in thermodynamics and heat (Q).
items.answer: Both are energy transfers: Q is transferred because of a temperature difference, while W is transferred by a force moving through a distance, such as a gas expanding against a piston.
items.markingKey: Both are energy transfers: Q is transferred because of a temperature difference, while W is transferred by a force moving through a distance, such as a gas expanding against a piston. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Arjun writes: "In the first law Q = ΔU + W, W is the work done on the gas." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In the IB convention, W is the work done by the gas; work done on the gas is −W.
items.markingKey: In the IB convention, W is the work done by the gas; work done on the gas is −W. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A gas in an insulated cylinder (no thermal energy transfer) is compressed by a piston that does 150 J of work on it. Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas.
A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the work done by the gas.
"The first law of thermodynamics means perpetual motion machines are impossible." Discuss.
items.answer: The first law rules out machines that create energy; the second law is needed to rule out those that turn heat completely into work.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a machine cannot output more energy than it receives (first-kind perpetual motion). Arguments against: the first law alone allows a machine converting heat fully to work – the second law forbids this; perpetual motion without output (frictionless) is allowed in principle. Supported judgement: The first law rules out machines that create energy; the second law is needed to rule out those that turn heat completely into work. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: In which process is no work done by the gas?
items.answer: Isovolumetric
items.markingKey: Isovolumetric (A1). ΔV = 0.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Isobaric means no work is done." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Isobaric means constant pressure; work pΔV is done if the volume changes. Isovolumetric processes involve no work.
items.markingKey: Isobaric means constant pressure; work pΔV is done if the volume changes. Isovolumetric processes involve no work. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a rapid compression can be modelled as adiabatic.
items.answer: Thermal energy transfer requires time; if the compression is very fast (or the gas well insulated) Q ≈ 0, so all work done on the gas increases its internal energy. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Thermal energy transfer requires time; if the compression is very fast (or the gas well insulated) Q ≈ 0, so all work done on the gas increases its internal energy. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: 1.0 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally at 350 K to 4 times its initial volume. Calculate the work done by the gas (W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)).
items.markingKey: W = nRT ln4 (M1) = 4030 J (A1); Q = W since ΔU = 0.

items.stem: A monatomic ideal gas at 280 K is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Calculate its final temperature.

1.00 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at A (1.00 × 10⁵ Pa, 320 K) undergoes a cycle: A→B isobaric expansion to 2 times the volume; B→C isovolumetric cooling back to 320 K; C→A isothermal compression to A. (a) Sketch the cycle on a p–V diagram. (b) Calculate the temperature at B and the pressure at C. (c) Calculate the work done in each stage. (d) Determine the net work done per cycle and the thermal energy absorbed in A→B. (e) Calculate the efficiency of the cycle.
items.markingKey: (a) A1. (b) A1 A1. (c) pΔV (A1), 0, nRT ln(V_C/V_A) (M1 A1). (d) W_net (A1), Q = (5/2)nRΔT (A1). (e) η = W/Q_in (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A graph of pressure against volume on which a process is shown as a curve and the work done is the area under it"?
items.answer: p–V diagram
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of p–V diagram.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes on p-V diagrams is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Priya.)
options: If the gas does at least as much work as the heat supplied (e.g. isothermal expansion), its internal energy and temperature need not rise.
Isobaric means no work is done.
Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases.
Entropy (J K⁻¹) measures the number of microscopic arrangements available, i.e. how dispersed energy is; it is not an amount of energy.
items.answer: Isobaric means no work is done.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Isobaric means constant pressure; work pΔV is done if the volume changes. Isovolumetric processes involve no work.

items.stem: In an isobaric expansion of an ideal gas, the temperature
items.answer: increases
items.markingKey: C. V ∝ T at constant p.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an isothermal process and an adiabatic process.
items.answer: In an isothermal process T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (heat flows in or out); in an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W and the temperature changes.
items.markingKey: In an isothermal process T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (heat flows in or out); in an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W and the temperature changes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Air in a syringe is compressed rapidly and the pressure is recorded with a fast pressure sensor at several volumes. For an adiabatic process pV^γ = constant, so ln p = −γ ln V + constant.

V / cm³ | p / kPa
50.0 | 99.7
45.0 | 116.2
40.0 | 137.0
35.0 | 165.0
30.0 | 203.6
25.0 | 264.1

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the adiabatic index γ of air. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State γ with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) ln p (y) against ln V (x); (b) gradient ≈ −1.40; (c) 1.40; (d) 1.40 ± 0.03
items.markingKey: (a) ln p (y) against ln V (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ −1.40 – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) γ = −gradient = 1.40 (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 0.03; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: An ideal gas is taken round a rectangular cycle on a p–V diagram between pressures 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa and volumes 0.00200 m³ and 0.00600 m³. Calculate the net work done per cycle.
items.markingKey: Net work = enclosed area = Δp × ΔV (M1) = 800 J (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes on p-V diagrams.

(a) An ideal monatomic gas at 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa expands adiabatically to 4 times its original volume. Calculate the final pressure (γ = 5/3). [2]

(b) Explain the difference between an isothermal process and an adiabatic process. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Real processes in engines can be described accurately as isothermal or adiabatic." [4]
items.answer: (a) 1.98 × 10⁴ Pa (b) In an isothermal process T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (heat flows in or out); in an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W and the temperature changes. (c) The idealised processes are useful models whose predictions must be corrected for real heat transfer and irreversibility.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] pV^γ constant (M1); p₂ = p₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 1.98 × 10⁴ Pa (A1). (b) [4 marks] In an isothermal process T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (heat flows in or out); in an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W and the temperature changes. (c) [4 marks] For: these idealisations allow simple calculations of work and efficiency; fast strokes are approximately adiabatic. Against: real processes are neither perfectly fast nor slow; heat leaks occur; friction and turbulence make processes irreversible; the gas composition changes during combustion. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The idealised processes are useful models whose predictions must be corrected for real heat transfer and irreversibility.

items.stem: "Real processes in engines can be described accurately as isothermal or adiabatic." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The idealised processes are useful models whose predictions must be corrected for real heat transfer and irreversibility.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: these idealisations allow simple calculations of work and efficiency; fast strokes are approximately adiabatic. Arguments against: real processes are neither perfectly fast nor slow; heat leaks occur; friction and turbulence make processes irreversible; the gas composition changes during combustion. items.stem: Define the term "macrostate".
items.answer: The state of a system described by macroscopic variables (p, V, T), corresponding to many microstates
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the state of a system described by macroscopic variables (p, V, T), corresponding to many microstates. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Heat flows from a hot body to a cold body because
items.answer: this increases the total entropy
items.markingKey: A. Second law.

items.stem: Distinguish between an irreversible process and a reversible process.
items.answer: A reversible process is an idealisation in which the system and surroundings can be returned to their original states with no net entropy change; real (irreversible) processes, involving friction, heat flow across finite temperature differences or free expansion, increase the total entropy.
items.markingKey: A reversible process is an idealisation in which the system and surroundings can be returned to their original states with no net entropy change; real (irreversible) processes, involving friction, heat flow across finite temperature differences or free expansion, increase the total entropy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Entropy can never decrease anywhere." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The entropy of a part of a system can decrease (e.g. freezing water) if the surroundings gain at least as much entropy; the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease.
items.markingKey: The entropy of a part of a system can decrease (e.g. freezing water) if the surroundings gain at least as much entropy; the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Calculate the entropy change when 0.1 kg of ice melts at 0 °C. (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
items.answer: 122 J K⁻¹

items.stem: 1000 J of thermal energy flows from a reservoir at 500 K to one at 280 K. Calculate the total change in entropy.

This question is about entropy and the second law of thermodynamics.

(a) The number of microstates of a system increases from 2.00 to 2.00 × 10¹⁰. Calculate the change in entropy using S = k_B ln Ω. [2]

(b) Explain the difference between a reversible process and an irreversible process. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "The second law of thermodynamics gives time its direction." [4]
items.answer: (a) 3.18 × 10⁻²² J K⁻¹ (b) A reversible process is an idealisation in which the system and surroundings can be returned to their original states with no net entropy change; real (irreversible) processes, involving friction, heat flow across finite temperature differences or free expansion, increase the total entropy. (c) The entropy increase provides a strong account of the arrow of time, but it depends on initial conditions and remains an active area of philosophical debate (TOK link).
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] ΔS = k_B ln(Ω₂/Ω₁) (M1) = 3.18 × 10⁻²² J K⁻¹ (A1). (b) [4 marks] A reversible process is an idealisation in which the system and surroundings can be returned to their original states with no net entropy change; real (irreversible) processes, involving friction, heat flow across finite temperature differences or free expansion, increase the total entropy. (c) [4 marks] For: irreversible processes (mixing, heat flow, ageing) all increase entropy; we never observe entropy decreasing spontaneously in isolated systems. Against: fundamental laws of mechanics are time-symmetric; the arrow depends on the universe’s special low-entropy initial state; other arrows (cosmological, psychological) have been proposed. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The entropy increase provides a strong account of the arrow of time, but it depends on initial conditions and remains an active area of philosophical debate (TOK link).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The second law of thermodynamics gives time its direction."
items.answer: The entropy increase provides a strong account of the arrow of time, but it depends on initial conditions and remains an active area of philosophical debate (TOK link).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: irreversible processes (mixing, heat flow, ageing) all increase entropy; we never observe entropy decreasing spontaneously in isolated systems. Arguments against: fundamental laws of mechanics are time-symmetric; the arrow depends on the universe’s special low-entropy initial state; other arrows (cosmological, psychological) have been proposed. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "entropy"?
options: A process at constant pressure, in which W = pΔV
A measure of the disorder of a system, related to the number of microstates Ω by S = k_B ln Ω
The thermal energy Q transferred to a system equals the increase in internal energy ΔU plus the work W done by the system: Q = ΔU + W
The ratio of the useful work output to the thermal energy input, η = W/Q_H
items.answer: A measure of the disorder of a system, related to the number of microstates Ω by S = k_B ln Ω
items.markingKey: B. "entropy" is a measure of the disorder of a system, related to the number of microstates Ω by S = k_B ln Ω.

items.stem: Clausius’s statement of the second law says that
options: heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body
items.answer: heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body
items.markingKey: B. Requires work to reverse.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a refrigerator does not violate the second law of thermodynamics.
items.answer: It transfers heat from cold to hot only because work is done on it; the heat released to the room exceeds that taken from inside, so the total entropy of the universe increases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It transfers heat from cold to hot only because work is done on it; the heat released to the room exceeds that taken from inside, so the total entropy of the universe increases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A teacher in Mexico City asks a class to choose the one correct statement about entropy and the second law of thermodynamics. Which statement should be chosen?
options: The heat rejected by a power station is a sign of poor engineering that can be eliminated.
Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases.
The second law means energy is lost.
In an adiabatic process the temperature stays constant.
items.answer: Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases.

items.stem: The number of microstates of a system increases from 2.00 to 2.00 × 10¹⁰. Calculate the change in entropy using S = k_B ln Ω.
items.markingKey: ΔS = k_B ln(Ω₂/Ω₁) (M1) = 3.18 × 10⁻²² J K⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: 2.26 × 10⁴ J of thermal energy is transferred reversibly into a large reservoir at 250 K. Calculate the entropy change of the reservoir.
Yusuf writes: "The second law means energy is lost." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases.
items.markingKey: Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 2000 J of thermal energy flows from a reservoir at 600 K to one at 300 K. Calculate the total change in entropy.

A 0.50 kg block of ice at 0 °C melts in a room at 22 °C. L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. (a) Calculate the energy absorbed by the ice. (b) Calculate the entropy change of the ice. (c) Calculate the entropy change of the room. (d) Show that the total entropy of the universe increases and explain the significance.
items.answer: (a) 1.67 × 10⁵ J; (b) +1.67 × 10⁵/273 = +612 J K⁻¹; (c) −1.67 × 10⁵/295 = −566 J K⁻¹; (d) net +46 J K⁻¹ > 0, consistent with the second law – heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.67 × 10⁵ J; (b) +1.67 × 10⁵/273 = +612 J K⁻¹; (c) −1.67 × 10⁵/295 = −566 J K⁻¹; (d) net +46 J K⁻¹ > 0, consistent with the second law – heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold.

items.answer: The entropy increase provides a strong account of the arrow of time, but it depends on initial conditions and remains an active area of philosophical debate (TOK link).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "thermal efficiency"?
options: The ratio of the useful work output to the thermal energy input, η = W/Q_H
A graph of pressure against volume on which a process is shown as a curve and the work done is the area under it
The maximum efficiency of any heat engine operating between reservoirs at T_H and T_C, η = 1 − T_C/T_H
The state of a system described by macroscopic variables (p, V, T), corresponding to many microstates
items.answer: The ratio of the useful work output to the thermal energy input, η = W/Q_H
items.markingKey: A. "thermal efficiency" is the ratio of the useful work output to the thermal energy input, η = W/Q_H.

items.stem: A heat engine would be 100 % efficient if
options: the hot reservoir were very hot
the cold reservoir were at 0 K
items.answer: the cold reservoir were at 0 K
items.markingKey: C. Carnot limit.

items.stem: A student claims: "A Carnot engine can reach 100 % efficiency if it has no friction." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Even an ideal, frictionless Carnot engine has η = 1 − T_C/T_H < 1, unless T_C = 0 K.
items.markingKey: Even an ideal, frictionless Carnot engine has η = 1 − T_C/T_H < 1, unless T_C = 0 K. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A power station near Toronto produces 500 MW of electrical power with an overall efficiency of 38 %. Calculate the rate at which thermal energy is rejected.
items.answer: 816 MW
items.markingKey: Input = 500/0.38 = 1320 MW (M1); rejected = 816 MW (A1).

items.stem: Calculate the Carnot efficiency of an engine operating between reservoirs at 800 K and 300 K.

This question is about heat engines, Carnot cycle and efficiency.

(a) A heat engine absorbs 800 J from the hot reservoir and does 280 J of work per cycle. Calculate the thermal energy rejected to the cold reservoir. [2]

(b) Distinguish between a heat pump and a heat engine. [4]

(c) "Combined heat and power (CHP) stations are a better use of fuel than conventional power stations." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of heat engines, Carnot cycle and efficiency. [4]
items.answer: (a) 520 J (b) A heat engine uses heat flowing from hot to cold to produce work; a heat pump uses work to move thermal energy from a cold to a hot region. (c) CHP makes much better use of fuel where there is a steady local heat demand, but it is not suitable everywhere.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Q_C = Q_H − W (M1) = 520 J (A1). (b) [4 marks] A heat engine uses heat flowing from hot to cold to produce work; a heat pump uses work to move thermal energy from a cold to a hot region. (c) [4 marks] For: use the rejected heat for district heating, raising total energy utilisation to ~80 %; reduce fuel use and emissions. Against: need nearby heat users (cities, industry); electrical efficiency may be slightly lower; heat demand varies seasonally. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: CHP makes much better use of fuel where there is a steady local heat demand, but it is not suitable everywhere.

items.stem: The Carnot cycle consists of
options: one of each type of process
two isothermal and two adiabatic processes
items.answer: two isothermal and two adiabatic processes
items.markingKey: D. Definition.

items.stem: Explain why no heat engine can be 100 % efficient.
items.answer: To return to its initial state in a cycle the engine must reject some thermal energy to a cold reservoir; rejecting no heat would decrease the total entropy, which the second law forbids. Efficiency 100 % would require T_C = 0 K.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To return to its initial state in a cycle the engine must reject some thermal energy to a cold reservoir; rejecting no heat would decrease the total entropy, which the second law forbids. Efficiency 100 % would require T_C = 0 K. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a heat engine and a heat pump.
items.answer: A heat engine uses heat flowing from hot to cold to produce work; a heat pump uses work to move thermal energy from a cold to a hot region.
items.markingKey: A heat engine uses heat flowing from hot to cold to produce work; a heat pump uses work to move thermal energy from a cold to a hot region. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A heat engine absorbs 2000 J from the hot reservoir and does 800 J of work per cycle. Calculate the thermal energy rejected to the cold reservoir.
Jonas writes: "In the Carnot efficiency formula, temperatures can be in °C." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Temperatures must be in kelvin; using °C gives wrong (even negative) efficiencies.
items.markingKey: Temperatures must be in kelvin; using °C gives wrong (even negative) efficiencies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A heat engine absorbs 1200 J from the hot reservoir and does 420 J of work per cycle. Calculate the thermal energy rejected to the cold reservoir.

A steam turbine operates between 820 K and 310 K. Its actual efficiency is 38 % and its electrical output is 600 MW. (a) Calculate the Carnot efficiency. (b) Calculate the thermal energy input per second. (c) Calculate the thermal energy rejected per second. (d) The rejected heat goes into river water; calculate the mass flow of water needed if its temperature may rise by only 8.0 K. (e) Suggest one way to increase the efficiency.
items.answer: (a) 62 %; (b) 1580 MW; (c) 980 MW; (d) 9.8 × 10⁸/(4180 × 8.0) = 2.9 × 10⁴ kg s⁻¹; (e) raise the steam temperature (superheating) or use combined cycle/CHP.
items.markingKey: (a) 62 %; (b) 1580 MW; (c) 980 MW; (d) 9.8 × 10⁸/(4180 × 8.0) = 2.9 × 10⁴ kg s⁻¹; (e) raise the steam temperature (superheating) or use combined cycle/CHP.

items.stem: "Combined heat and power (CHP) stations are a better use of fuel than conventional power stations." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: CHP makes much better use of fuel where there is a steady local heat demand, but it is not suitable everywhere.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The state of a system described by macroscopic variables (p, V, T), corresponding to many microstates"?
items.answer: macrostate
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of macrostate.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "first law of thermodynamics".
items.answer: The thermal energy Q transferred to a system equals the increase in internal energy ΔU plus the work W done by the system: Q = ΔU + W
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the thermal energy Q transferred to a system equals the increase in internal energy ΔU plus the work W done by the system: Q = ΔU + W. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

options: steeper than an isothermal curve through the same point
items.answer: steeper than an isothermal curve through the same point

items.stem: A student in Vienna is checking notes on heat engines, Carnot cycle and efficiency. Which statement is incorrect?
options: A Carnot engine can reach 100 % efficiency if it has no friction.
Entropy (J K⁻¹) measures the number of microscopic arrangements available, i.e. how dispersed energy is; it is not an amount of energy.
Temperatures must be in kelvin; using °C gives wrong (even negative) efficiencies.
Some heat rejection is required by the second law; engineering can only reduce it towards the Carnot limit (or use the waste heat in combined heat and power).
items.answer: A Carnot engine can reach 100 % efficiency if it has no friction.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: Even an ideal, frictionless Carnot engine has η = 1 − T_C/T_H < 1, unless T_C = 0 K.

items.stem: Explain why living organisms do not violate the second law even though they create ordered structures.
items.answer: Organisms are open systems; they take in low-entropy energy (food, sunlight) and release heat and waste that increase the entropy of the surroundings by more than their internal decrease.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Organisms are open systems; they take in low-entropy energy (food, sunlight) and release heat and waste that increase the entropy of the surroundings by more than their internal decrease. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.markingKey: B. Isothermal: U constant.

items.answer: an isovolumetric process

items.stem: Which of the following statements about heat engines, Carnot cycle and efficiency is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Yusuf.)
options: Isobaric means constant pressure; work pΔV is done if the volume changes. Isovolumetric processes involve no work.
The heat rejected by a power station is a sign of poor engineering that can be eliminated.
Temperatures must be in kelvin; using °C gives wrong (even negative) efficiencies.
If the gas does at least as much work as the heat supplied (e.g. isothermal expansion), its internal energy and temperature need not rise.
items.answer: The heat rejected by a power station is a sign of poor engineering that can be eliminated.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Some heat rejection is required by the second law; engineering can only reduce it towards the Carnot limit (or use the waste heat in combined heat and power).

items.stem: A teacher in Mumbai asks a class to choose the one correct statement about entropy and the second law of thermodynamics. Which statement should be chosen?
options: Entropy (J K⁻¹) measures the number of microscopic arrangements available, i.e. how dispersed energy is; it is not an amount of energy.
In an isothermal expansion no heat is transferred because the temperature does not change.
Supplying heat to a gas always increases its temperature.
A system contains a certain amount of heat.
items.answer: Entropy (J K⁻¹) measures the number of microscopic arrangements available, i.e. how dispersed energy is; it is not an amount of energy.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. Entropy (J K⁻¹) measures the number of microscopic arrangements available, i.e. how dispersed energy is; it is not an amount of energy.

items.stem: A gas absorbs 500 J of thermal energy while doing 400 J of work on its surroundings. Calculate the change in its internal energy.
items.markingKey: ΔU = Q − W with W = 400 J (M1); ΔU = 100 J (A1).

items.markingKey: C. W = nRT ln2 (M1) = 4030 J (A1); Q = W since ΔU = 0.

items.answer: Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases.
items.markingKey: Energy is conserved (first law); the second law says energy becomes less available for doing work as entropy increases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: B. ΔU = Q − W with W = −600 J (M1); ΔU = 950 J (A1).

items.stem:
Air in a syringe is compressed rapidly and the pressure is recorded with a fast pressure sensor at several volumes. For an adiabatic process pV^γ = constant, so ln p = −γ ln V + constant.

V / cm³ | p / kPa
50.0 | 99.6
45.0 | 115.4
40.0 | 135.9
35.0 | 163.9
30.0 | 201.7
25.0 | 258.4

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the adiabatic index γ of air. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State γ with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) ln p (y) against ln V (x); (b) gradient ≈ −1.38; (c) 1.38; (d) 1.38 ± 0.06

This question is about entropy and the second law of thermodynamics.

(a) Calculate the entropy change when 0.5 kg of ice melts at 0 °C. (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹) [2]

(b) Distinguish between a reversible process and an irreversible process. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "The second law of thermodynamics gives time its direction." [4]
items.answer: (a) 612 J K⁻¹ (b) A reversible process is an idealisation in which the system and surroundings can be returned to their original states with no net entropy change; real (irreversible) processes, involving friction, heat flow across finite temperature differences or free expansion, increase the total entropy. (c) The entropy increase provides a strong account of the arrow of time, but it depends on initial conditions and remains an active area of philosophical debate (TOK link).
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] ΔS = mL/T = 0.5 × 3.34 × 10⁵/273 (M1) = 612 J K⁻¹ (A1). (b) [4 marks] A reversible process is an idealisation in which the system and surroundings can be returned to their original states with no net entropy change; real (irreversible) processes, involving friction, heat flow across finite temperature differences or free expansion, increase the total entropy. (c) [4 marks] For: irreversible processes (mixing, heat flow, ageing) all increase entropy; we never observe entropy decreasing spontaneously in isolated systems. Against: fundamental laws of mechanics are time-symmetric; the arrow depends on the universe’s special low-entropy initial state; other arrows (cosmological, psychological) have been proposed. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The entropy increase provides a strong account of the arrow of time, but it depends on initial conditions and remains an active area of philosophical debate (TOK link).

items.stem:
This question is about first law of thermodynamics, work done by a gas and internal energy.

(a) 1.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 60 K. Calculate the thermal energy supplied. [3]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain, using the first law, why a gas cools when it expands rapidly. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "The first law of thermodynamics means perpetual motion machines are impossible." [4]
items.answer: (a) 1250 J (b) In a rapid expansion there is little time for thermal energy transfer (Q ≈ 0); the gas does work on the surroundings, so ΔU = −W is negative and its temperature falls. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) The first law rules out machines that create energy; the second law is needed to rule out those that turn heat completely into work.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, W = pΔV = nRΔT (M1); Q = (5/2)nRΔT = 1250 J (A1). (b) [3 marks] In a rapid expansion there is little time for thermal energy transfer (Q ≈ 0); the gas does work on the surroundings, so ΔU = −W is negative and its temperature falls. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: a machine cannot output more energy than it receives (first-kind perpetual motion). Against: the first law alone allows a machine converting heat fully to work – the second law forbids this; perpetual motion without output (frictionless) is allowed in principle. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The first law rules out machines that create energy; the second law is needed to rule out those that turn heat completely into work.

items.stem: 1.00 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-quarter of its volume. (a) Calculate the initial volume. (b) Calculate the final pressure and temperature. (c) Calculate the work done on the gas. (d) Compare the final pressure with that for an isothermal compression to the same volume and explain the difference.
items.answer: (a) V = nRT/p = 0.0249 m³; (b) p₂ = p₁ × 4^(5/3) = 1.01 × 10⁶ Pa, T₂ = 300 × 4^(2/3) = 756 K; (c) W_on = ΔU = 1.5 × 8.31 × 456 = 5.68 kJ; (d) isothermal gives 4.00 × 10⁵ Pa; the adiabatic pressure is higher because the temperature also rises.
items.markingKey: (a) V = nRT/p = 0.0249 m³; (b) p₂ = p₁ × 4^(5/3) = 1.01 × 10⁶ Pa, T₂ = 300 × 4^(2/3) = 756 K; (c) W_on = ΔU = 1.5 × 8.31 × 456 = 5.68 kJ; (d) isothermal gives 4.00 × 10⁵ Pa; the adiabatic pressure is higher because the temperature also rises.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "macrostate"?

A measure of the disorder of a system, related to the number of microstates Ω by S = k_B ln Ω
A change of state of a system, described by changes in p, V and T

items.answer: The state of a system described by macroscopic variables (p, V, T), corresponding to many microstates

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "isovolumetric (isochoric) process"?
options: A change of state of a system, described by changes in p, V and T
A process at constant volume, in which no work is done and Q = ΔU
A device that takes in thermal energy from a hot reservoir, converts part of it into work and rejects the rest to a cold reservoir
A measure of the disorder of a system, related to the number of microstates Ω by S = k_B ln Ω
items.answer: A process at constant volume, in which no work is done and Q = ΔU
items.markingKey: B. "isovolumetric (isochoric) process" is a process at constant volume, in which no work is done and Q = ΔU.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a heat engine and a heat pump.
items.answer: A heat engine uses heat flowing from hot to cold to produce work; a heat pump uses work to move thermal energy from a cold to a hot region.

items.stem: Distinguish between heat (Q) and work (W) in thermodynamics.
items.answer: Both are energy transfers: Q is transferred because of a temperature difference, while W is transferred by a force moving through a distance, such as a gas expanding against a piston.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a rapid compression can be modelled as adiabatic.
items.answer: Thermal energy transfer requires time; if the compression is very fast (or the gas well insulated) Q ≈ 0, so all work done on the gas increases its internal energy.

items.stem: Briefly explain why power stations are built next to rivers or the sea.
items.answer: They need a large cold reservoir to absorb the rejected thermal energy; the lower T_C, the higher the possible efficiency.

items.stem:
This question is about first law of thermodynamics, work done by a gas and internal energy.

(a) A gas in an insulated cylinder (no thermal energy transfer) is compressed by a piston that does 150 J of work on it. Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas. [2]

(b) Explain the difference between work (W) in thermodynamics and heat (Q). [4]

(c) "The first law of thermodynamics means perpetual motion machines are impossible." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of first law of thermodynamics, work done by a gas and internal energy. [4]
items.answer: (a) 150 J (b) Both are energy transfers: Q is transferred because of a temperature difference, while W is transferred by a force moving through a distance, such as a gas expanding against a piston. (c) The first law rules out machines that create energy; the second law is needed to rule out those that turn heat completely into work.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Q = 0; W (by gas) = −150 J (M1); ΔU = Q − W = +150 J (A1). (b) [4 marks] Both are energy transfers: Q is transferred because of a temperature difference, while W is transferred by a force moving through a distance, such as a gas expanding against a piston. (c) [4 marks] For: a machine cannot output more energy than it receives (first-kind perpetual motion). Against: the first law alone allows a machine converting heat fully to work – the second law forbids this; perpetual motion without output (frictionless) is allowed in principle. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The first law rules out machines that create energy; the second law is needed to rule out those that turn heat completely into work.

items.stem:
This question is about isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes on p-V diagrams.

(a) A monatomic ideal gas at 280 K is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Calculate its final temperature. [2]

(b) Distinguish between an isothermal process and an adiabatic process. [4]

(c) "Real processes in engines can be described accurately as isothermal or adiabatic." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes on p-V diagrams. [4]
items.answer: (a) 1120 K (b) In an isothermal process T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (heat flows in or out); in an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W and the temperature changes. (c) The idealised processes are useful models whose predictions must be corrected for real heat transfer and irreversibility.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] TV^(γ−1) constant (M1); T₂ = 280 × 8^(2/3) = 1120 K (A1). (b) [4 marks] In an isothermal process T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (heat flows in or out); in an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W and the temperature changes. (c) [4 marks] For: these idealisations allow simple calculations of work and efficiency; fast strokes are approximately adiabatic. Against: real processes are neither perfectly fast nor slow; heat leaks occur; friction and turbulence make processes irreversible; the gas composition changes during combustion. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The idealised processes are useful models whose predictions must be corrected for real heat transfer and irreversibility.

items.answer: (a) 41.7 % (b) Real cycles are irreversible: friction, turbulence and heat transfer across finite temperature differences increase entropy, and the processes are not ideal isotherms and adiabats. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) CHP makes much better use of fuel where there is a steady local heat demand, but it is not suitable everywhere.

(b) [3 marks] Real cycles are irreversible: friction, turbulence and heat transfer across finite temperature differences increase entropy, and the processes are not ideal isotherms and adiabats. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [6 marks] For: use the rejected heat for district heating, raising total energy utilisation to ~80 %; reduce fuel use and emissions. Against: need nearby heat users (cities, industry); electrical efficiency may be slightly lower; heat demand varies seasonally. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: CHP makes much better use of fuel where there is a steady local heat demand, but it is not suitable everywhere.
